definition: Raze means to tear a structure down completely to the ground.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word raze. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know raze should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Wrecking crews razed the empty cannery in nine days, and by spring only a gravel pad marked the block.
Damage is the loosest rung — anything from a cracked pane to a burnt wing, with the building still a building — while raze ends the scale with the whole structure brought down to the ground.
Gut goes further than damage — the whole interior is destroyed even while the shell stands — but raze claims the most: nothing left upright at all.

Demolish is the engineer's everyday word for tearing built things down on purpose, and it is satisfied by the act at any size — you can demolish one wall and keep the house. Raze accepts nothing partial: a razed site reads as ground, nothing left standing.

To level a building is to bring it flat with the ground, and the word stays as calm as a surveyor's tool. Raze means the same flattening with the violence left showing — fire-hooks, wrecking balls, a structure deliberately brought to nothing — which is why headlines reach for it.

When the Great Fire of 1666 outran London's bucket lines, the king's men stopped fighting the flames and started starving them: with fire-hooks and axes they razed whole streets of untouched houses ahead of the blaze, pulling roofs and timbers flat so the fire would arrive and find nothing standing to feed on.
Householders wept, and helped.
The gaps worked where the water had not.
Raze is the exact word for that tactic, because it means to tear a structure down completely to the ground — the phrase razed to the ground is nearly one word in English.
Demolish shares the work but not the emphasis; you can demolish a wall and keep the house.
Raze insists on level: when the crews finish, the site reads as ground, not as building.
Raze is a whole-structure verb: buildings, blocks, fortresses brought level with the ground — headline writers love its four ruthless letters.
Demolish is the engineer's everyday word; level, the plain one.
In this unit's division of labor, pillage empties a place and leaves it standing; raze leaves nothing standing; obliterate erases even the trace that it stood.

When the interstate came through in 1962, the Hayti district -- four churches, a theater, three hundred houses -- stood directly in the surveyed path.
City files called the work 'clearance,' but residents used a harder word: the neighborhood was to be razed, brought entirely to the ground.
Wrecking crews worked west to east for two years, and when they finished, not a porch step or a corner store remained.
Families scattered to whatever housing they could find, holding deeds to lots that no longer had addresses.
Decades later, a single historical marker beside the off-ramp is all that stands where the district's main street began.
